noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: describe the role of ADH in regulating the water content of the blood
understand that urine contains water, urea and ions

primer.text: You have already met the nephron and seen that most water leaves the filtrate through the collecting duct. This note adds the hormone that supervises that water exit — antidiuretic hormone — and then asks what the fluid that finally reaches the bladder is actually made of. Master both halves and the kidney's water story is complete.

lessons.title: The Role of ADH
lessons.opening: Antidiuretic hormone is the body's water-balancing lever. Detectors in the brain sense how watery the blood is, the pituitary adjusts how much ADH it releases, and the collecting duct answers by changing how easily water slips back into the bloodstream. When blood water rises above the set point, ADH output falls and a big volume of watery urine carries the surplus away; when blood water falls, ADH rises and only a small, concentrated sample is lost. The loop is a classic negative-feedback system.
keyPoints: Osmoregulation means keeping the water and salt content of the body steady.
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus monitor how much water the blood is carrying.
The hypothalamus instructs the pituitary gland, which secretes ADH into the blood.
ADH makes the collecting duct more permeable, so more water leaves the filtrate.
A drop in blood water triggers a larger ADH release and a more concentrated urine.
The loop is negative feedback: the correction always opposes the drift.

low.restatement: ADH is the hormone that decides how much water the kidney takes back from the filtrate.
low.analogy: Think of ADH as the tap handle on a bath: turn it up and more water is kept in, turn it down and the water drains away.
low.examPointer: Always state the direction plainly: more ADH opens the duct to water — mark schemes reward the exact mechanism.

medium.restatement: Too little blood water means more ADH and concentrated urine; too much means less ADH and dilute urine.
medium.analogy: It works like a thermostat, but for water instead of warmth: the sensor notices the drift and the pituitary answers it.
medium.examPointer: Quote the direction of both changes — ADH release and duct permeability — for full marks.

check.stem: Which change in ADH release follows when the water potential of the blood climbs too high?

options.text: The pituitary releases less ADH
options.explanation: Extra blood water means the correction is to keep less water, so ADH output falls.

options.text: The pituitary releases more ADH
options.explanation: More ADH would reclaim even more water, worsening the surplus rather than correcting it.

options.text: ADH release stops permanently
options.explanation: The system dials ADH down gradually; it does not switch off altogether.

options.text: ADH release stays exactly the same
options.explanation: A feedback system responds to the drift; an unchanged ADH level would leave the imbalance uncorrected.

check.stem: What direct effect does ADH have on the collecting duct?

options.text: Its walls become more permeable to water
options.explanation: ADH acts on the duct walls so water can leave the filtrate more freely.

options.text: Its walls become less permeable to water
options.explanation: That is the response when ADH is withdrawn, not when it is present.

options.text: Its walls become thicker to slow filtration
options.explanation: ADH changes permeability, not wall thickness, and filtration happens in the glomerulus.

options.text: It pumps water into the duct by active transport
options.explanation: Water leaves the duct by osmosis; active transport is the glucose story in the PCT.

check.stem: Where are the detectors that monitor blood water concentration located?

options.text: In the hypothalamus of the brain
options.explanation: Osmoreceptors sit in the hypothalamus and watch the blood's water content.

options.text: In the collecting duct of each nephron
options.explanation: The duct is where water is reabsorbed, not where the change is detected.

options.text: In the renal pelvis of the kidney
options.explanation: The renal pelvis gathers urine; it plays no sensing role.

options.text: In the ureter walls
options.explanation: The ureter only transports urine towards the bladder.

check.stem: A hiker has sweated heavily on a long walk and drinks nothing. Which urine output would you expect?

options.text: A small volume of dark, concentrated urine
options.explanation: Sweating loses water, so ADH rises, plenty is reabsorbed, and little concentrated urine remains.

options.text: A large volume of pale, dilute urine
options.explanation: Dilute, plentiful urine appears when blood water is in surplus, the opposite of dehydration.

options.text: No urine at all
options.explanation: Waste must still be removed; output shrinks but never stops.

options.text: Urine with no urea in it
options.explanation: Urea is always excreted; only the water fraction changes.

check.stem: Which statement about the ADH feedback loop is correct?

options.text: A fall in blood water raises ADH, which lets the duct reclaim more water
options.explanation: Low blood water triggers a bigger ADH release and therefore greater reabsorption.

options.text: A fall in blood water lowers ADH, so the duct loses more water
options.explanation: Both halves are inverted; the loop actually defends the water the body has.

options.text: A rise in blood water raises ADH, so the duct reclaims more
options.explanation: A surplus suppresses ADH rather than boosting it.

options.text: ADH alters how much filtrate the glomerulus makes
options.explanation: Filtration rate at the glomerulus is not what ADH controls; the duct is.

check.stem: Name the hormone that controls how much water is reabsorbed from the collecting duct.
check.modelAnswer: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH), released by the pituitary gland.

check.stem: State the exact effect ADH has on the collecting duct.
check.modelAnswer: ADH makes the collecting duct more permeable to water.

check.stem: Explain why the ADH system is described as negative feedback.
check.modelAnswer: Because a move away from the normal blood water level triggers a response that pushes it back: low water raises ADH so more is reabsorbed, high water lowers ADH so more is lost, and the correction always opposes the original change.

check.stem: On a hot sports day a runner drinks very little. Describe the full sequence from detection to urine output.
check.modelAnswer: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the concentrated blood, the pituitary releases more ADH, the walls of the collecting ducts open up to water, extra water is reabsorbed into the blood, and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced.

lessons.title: The Composition of Urine
lessons.opening: Everything the kidney decides ends up dissolved in the urine it hands to the bladder. Its three ingredients — water, urea and ions — appear in proportions that shift with drinking, weather and exercise. After a long flight spent sipping water you produce generous, pale urine; after a match played in the sun you produce a small, dark sample. The colour of the sample tells the story before any test does.
keyPoints: Urine is a solution of water, urea and excess ions.
Plentiful pale urine means the urea in it is diluted; scanty dark urine means it is concentrated.
Drinking more water produces a larger volume of paler urine.
Hot conditions or hard exercise shift water into sweat, shrinking and darkening the urine.
The kidneys adjust these proportions continuously as part of osmoregulation.

low.restatement: Urine carries water, urea and ions, and its colour shows how concentrated it is.
low.analogy: It is like squash in a glass: more water added, the colour fades; less water, the colour deepens.
low.examPointer: Link each cause — intake, temperature, exercise — to the volume and colour change it produces.

medium.restatement: More drinking gives pale, plentiful urine; heat or exercise gives dark, scanty urine.
medium.analogy: Picture a kettle boiling away water: what is left behind becomes stronger and darker.
medium.examPointer: Practise writing cause-and-effect chains from each trigger to the final urine description.

check.stem: Which three substances does urine contain?

options.text: Water, urea and ions
options.explanation: These are the three components named in the specification.

options.text: Glucose, protein and water
options.explanation: Healthy urine contains no glucose or protein; both are reabsorbed or too large to filter.

options.text: Water, urea and red blood cells
options.explanation: Blood cells stay in the blood; they never cross the filter.

options.text: Urea only, dissolved in plasma
options.explanation: Urea travels in water with ions; plasma is not excreted as such.

check.stem: Why is urine passed after strenuous exercise usually darker in colour?

options.text: Water lost in sweat leaves less to dilute the urea
options.explanation: Exercise raises sweat loss, so the remaining urine is concentrated and darker.

options.text: Exercise makes the kidneys produce extra urea
options.explanation: The urea load hardly changes; it is the water fraction that falls.

options.text: Exercise damages the filters so protein leaks out
options.explanation: Protein leakage is a high-blood-pressure effect on the glomerulus, not a normal exercise outcome.

options.text: Exercise stops ADH release completely
options.explanation: Dehydration raises ADH; it does not abolish it.

check.stem: A person spends an afternoon drinking large amounts of water. Which urine description fits?

options.text: Large quantity, pale yellow
options.explanation: Surplus water is excreted, so volume rises and the urea is diluted to a pale colour.

options.text: Small quantity, dark yellow
options.explanation: That is the dehydration picture, not the over-hydration one.

options.text: Large quantity, dark yellow
options.explanation: The volume is right but the colour is wrong; extra water lightens the sample.

options.text: Normal quantity with visible ions settled out
options.explanation: Ions stay dissolved; they do not settle out of urine.

check.stem: Which factor does NOT directly change the concentration of urine?

options.text: The colour of the clothing worn
options.explanation: Clothing colour has no role in the water balance described here.

options.text: The amount of fluid drunk
options.explanation: Intake directly dilutes or concentrates the urine.

options.text: The surrounding temperature
options.explanation: Heat drives sweat loss and concentrates urine.

options.text: The level of physical activity
options.explanation: Exercise drives sweat loss in the same direction.

check.stem: What happens to the urea in urine when the urine volume is large and pale?

options.text: It is less concentrated because it is dissolved in more water
options.explanation: A bigger water fraction spreads the same urea more thinly.

options.text: It becomes more concentrated
options.explanation: More water means less concentrated urea, not more.

options.text: It disappears entirely
options.explanation: Urea is always present; dilution is not removal.

options.text: It turns into ions
options.explanation: Urea and ions are separate solutes; neither converts into the other.

check.stem: List the three components of urine.
check.modelAnswer: Urine contains water, urea and ions.

check.stem: State two everyday factors that make urine more concentrated.
check.modelAnswer: High temperature and vigorous exercise, because both increase the water lost as sweat.

check.stem: Explain why someone who drinks very little on a warm day produces dark urine.
check.modelAnswer: Warm conditions and low intake together leave the blood short of water, so ADH rises and the collecting duct reclaims most of it; the small volume of urine left carries the usual urea in much less water, so it looks dark.

check.stem: Two athletes finish the same match: one drank two litres during play, one drank nothing. Predict and explain each urine output.
check.modelAnswer: The drinker passes a large volume of pale urine because surplus water suppresses ADH and dilutes the urea; the non-drinker passes a small volume of dark urine because sweat loss raised ADH, the duct reabsorbed heavily, and the remaining urea is concentrated.

glossary.definition: Antidiuretic hormone, released by the pituitary gland; it raises the water permeability of the collecting duct.
The maintenance of steady water and salt levels in the body fluids.
A sensory cell in the hypothalamus that monitors the water content of the blood.
A control loop in which the response opposes the original change, returning the condition to its set point.

figures.alt: Body response to low blood water: detection in the hypothalamus, ADH release, increased kidney reabsorption.
figures.caption: The feedback sequence that restores blood water when it runs low

figures.alt: Body response to surplus blood water: reduced ADH release and reduced kidney reabsorption.
figures.caption: The mirror-image sequence when the blood carries too much water
